stem: What is the formula for an object's linear momentum?

choices.label: A
choices.text: $p = mv$, where m is mass and v is velocity
choices.explanation: Momentum is defined as mass times velocity.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This is the formula for kinetic energy, not momentum.

choices.label: C
choices.text: $p = ma$
choices.explanation: This is the formula for net force (Newton's Second Law), not momentum.

choices.label: D
choices.text: $p = m/v$
choices.explanation: Momentum is the PRODUCT of mass and velocity, not their quotient.

explanation: Momentum is p = mv.

stem: A 5 kg object moves at 10 m/s. What is its momentum?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 50 kg·m/s

choices.label: B
choices.text: 15 kg·m/s
choices.explanation: This adds mass and velocity rather than multiplying them.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 2 kg·m/s
choices.explanation: This incorrectly divides mass by velocity rather than multiplying them.

choices.label: D
choices.text: 0.5 kg·m/s
choices.explanation: This incorrectly divides velocity by mass rather than multiplying them.

stem: What does the Impulse-Momentum Theorem state?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Impulse (force times time) equals the change in momentum: $J = F\Delta t = \Delta p$
choices.explanation: This is the standard statement of the impulse-momentum theorem.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Impulse equals the object's total kinetic energy
choices.explanation: Impulse relates to the CHANGE IN MOMENTUM, not kinetic energy.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Impulse is always zero for any collision
choices.explanation: Impulse is generally nonzero whenever a force acts over some time interval, changing an object's momentum.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Impulse equals mass divided by time
choices.explanation: Impulse is force multiplied by time (J=FΔt), not mass divided by time.

explanation: The Impulse-Momentum Theorem: J = FΔt = Δp.

stem: A force of 20 N is applied to an object for 3 seconds. What impulse does this deliver?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 60 N·s

choices.label: B
choices.text: 23 N·s
choices.explanation: This adds force and time rather than multiplying them.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This incorrectly divides force by time rather than multiplying them.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This incorrectly divides time by force rather than multiplying them.

stem: A 5 kg object receives an impulse of 60 N·s. By how much does its velocity change?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 12 m/s

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This incorrectly multiplies J and m rather than dividing J by m.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 55 m/s
choices.explanation: This subtracts m from J rather than dividing.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This incorrectly divides m by J rather than J by m.

stem: Is momentum a vector or a scalar quantity?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A vector -- it has both magnitude and direction
choices.explanation: Momentum (p=mv) inherits the vector nature of velocity, so it has both magnitude and direction.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A scalar -- it only has magnitude, no direction
choices.explanation: Momentum is a vector because it's derived from velocity (a vector), and it has a meaningful direction.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Neither -- momentum has no mathematical properties
choices.explanation: Momentum is a well-defined physical quantity with clear mathematical (vector) properties.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It depends on whether the object is moving in a straight line
choices.explanation: Momentum is always a vector, regardless of whether the motion happens to be along a straight line or not.

explanation: Momentum is a vector quantity, with both magnitude and direction, since it depends on velocity.

stem: A 2 kg object moving at 5 m/s experiences a force of -10 N for 2 seconds (opposing its motion). What is its velocity after this force acts?

choices.label: A
choices.text: -5 m/s (i.e., 5 m/s in the reversed direction)
choices.explanation: J = FΔt = (-10)(2) = -20 N·s = Δp. Δv = Δp/m = -20/2 = -10 m/s. Final velocity: v = v0 + Δv = 5 + (-10) = -5 m/s.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 0 m/s (the object comes to rest)
choices.explanation: The force is large enough to not just stop the object but actually reverse its direction of motion.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 15 m/s
choices.explanation: This incorrectly adds rather than accounts for the negative (opposing) impulse's effect on velocity.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This is the CHANGE in velocity (Δv), not the final velocity (which is v0 + Δv).

explanation: Δv = J/m = -20/2 = -10 m/s. Final velocity = 5 + (-10) = -5 m/s -- the object's direction reverses.

stem: Why do airbags and crumple zones in cars reduce the force experienced during a collision, even though the change in momentum (impulse) is the same?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They increase the time (Δt) over which the momentum change occurs, and since $F=\Delta p/\Delta t$, a longer time means a smaller average force for the same Δp
choices.explanation: Since impulse (Δp) is fixed by the collision's physics, stretching out the time reduces the average force needed to produce that same impulse.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They reduce the total change in momentum
choices.explanation: The change in momentum (determined by the mass and how much the velocity changes) is essentially the same regardless of airbags -- what changes is the TIME over which it happens, not the momentum change itself.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They increase the mass of the car, reducing acceleration
choices.explanation: Airbags and crumple zones don't meaningfully change the car's mass -- they work by extending the collision TIME, not by adding mass.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They have no real effect on the force experienced
choices.explanation: Airbags and crumple zones do meaningfully reduce force, by extending the time over which the momentum change occurs.

explanation: Airbags/crumple zones extend the collision time Δt; since F=Δp/Δt and Δp is fixed, a longer Δt means a smaller average force.

stem: What does the Law of Conservation of Momentum state?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In the absence of external forces, the total momentum of a system remains constant
choices.explanation: This is the standard statement of conservation of momentum -- total momentum before equals total momentum after, if no external force acts.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Momentum is always zero for any isolated system
choices.explanation: Momentum can be any nonzero constant value for an isolated system -- conservation means it stays CONSTANT, not that it's necessarily zero.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Momentum increases over time for any system
choices.explanation: Without external forces, momentum stays CONSTANT, it doesn't systematically increase.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Only kinetic energy is conserved, not momentum
choices.explanation: This is backwards for general collisions -- momentum is ALWAYS conserved in isolated systems, while kinetic energy is only conserved in elastic collisions.

explanation: Conservation of momentum: in the absence of external forces, total momentum of a system stays constant.

stem: A 3 kg cart moving at 4 m/s collides with a stationary 2 kg cart, and they stick together (perfectly inelastic collision). What is their combined velocity after the collision?

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: By conservation of momentum: (3)(4)+(2)(0) = (3+2)v_f, so 12 = 5v_f, giving v_f = 2.4 m/s.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 4 m/s
choices.explanation: This ignores the added mass of the stationary cart, which slows the combined system down.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 6 m/s
choices.explanation: This doesn't correctly apply conservation of momentum -- the combined velocity must be LESS than the initial 4 m/s, since mass increased with no added momentum.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This is half the correct value -- possibly from a division error.

explanation: Total momentum before = (3)(4) = 12 kg·m/s. After sticking together: 12 = (3+2)v_f, so v_f = 2.4 m/s.

stem: Two carts, initially at rest and touching, push apart (like a small explosion). Cart 1 ($m_1=2$ kg) ends up moving at 6 m/s. Cart 2 has mass $m_2=3$ kg. What is Cart 2's velocity?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 4 m/s, in the opposite direction from Cart 1
choices.explanation: Total momentum starts at zero: 0 = m1v1+m2v2, so v2 = -m1v1/m2 = -(2)(6)/3 = -4 m/s -- 4 m/s opposite to Cart 1's direction.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 4 m/s, in the same direction as Cart 1
choices.explanation: For total momentum to remain zero, Cart 2 must move in the OPPOSITE direction from Cart 1, not the same direction.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 6 m/s, in the opposite direction from Cart 1
choices.explanation: This doesn't correctly account for the different masses of the two carts -- the lighter cart (Cart 1) must move faster than the heavier cart (Cart 2).

choices.label: D
choices.text: 9 m/s, in the opposite direction from Cart 1
choices.explanation: This doesn't correctly solve m1v1=-m2v2 for v2 using the given masses and Cart 1's velocity.

explanation: Since total momentum starts and remains zero: m1v1+m2v2=0, so v2 = -(2)(6)/3 = -4 m/s (opposite direction).

stem: Is momentum conserved in a collision even if kinetic energy is NOT conserved (i.e., an inelastic collision)?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Yes -- momentum is conserved in ALL collisions (elastic or inelastic), as long as there's no external force; kinetic energy conservation is a separate, additional condition that only holds for elastic collisions
choices.explanation: Momentum conservation is a much more general principle than kinetic energy conservation -- it holds for all types of collisions, while KE conservation only holds for elastic collisions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No -- momentum is only conserved when kinetic energy is also conserved
choices.explanation: This is a common misconception -- momentum conservation and kinetic energy conservation are independent conditions; momentum is conserved much more broadly.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Momentum is never conserved in any real collision
choices.explanation: Momentum IS conserved in essentially all collisions where no external force acts, regardless of whether they're elastic or inelastic.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Only kinetic energy is conserved; momentum is never relevant to collisions
choices.explanation: This has it backward -- momentum is the quantity that's always conserved in collisions (absent external forces), while KE conservation is the special, additional case.

explanation: Momentum is conserved in ALL collisions (given no external force), regardless of whether kinetic energy is also conserved.

stem: A 2 kg gun fires a 0.01 kg bullet at a muzzle velocity of 400 m/s. Using conservation of momentum, what is the gun's recoil velocity?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 2 m/s, in the direction opposite the bullet
choices.explanation: Total momentum starts at zero: 0 = m_bullet·v_bullet + m_gun·v_gun, so v_gun = -(0.01)(400)/2 = -2 m/s.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 4 m/s, in the direction opposite the bullet
choices.explanation: This doesn't correctly divide the bullet's momentum by the gun's mass (2 kg).

choices.label: C
choices.text: 400 m/s, in the direction opposite the bullet
choices.explanation: This is the bullet's speed, not the (much smaller, since the gun is much more massive) recoil speed of the gun.

choices.label: D
choices.text: 0.02 m/s, in the direction opposite the bullet
choices.explanation: This doesn't correctly compute the bullet's momentum (0.01×400=4 kg·m/s) before dividing by the gun's mass.

explanation: Setting total momentum to zero: v_gun = -(m_bullet·v_bullet)/m_gun = -(0.01)(400)/2 = -2 m/s.

stem: Why is momentum conserved during a collision between two objects that exert forces on each other, even though each object individually experiences a (possibly large) force during the collision?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The forces the two objects exert on each other are internal to the system and form a Newton's Third Law pair (equal and opposite), so they cancel out when considering the system's total momentum
choices.explanation: Internal forces between colliding objects are Third Law pairs; when analyzing the combined system, these internal forces cancel, leaving total momentum unchanged (absent external forces).

choices.label: B
choices.text: The forces during a collision are always zero
choices.explanation: Collision forces are often very large (not zero) -- but since they're internal (Third Law) pairs, they cancel for the SYSTEM's total momentum, even though they strongly affect each individual object.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Momentum conservation has nothing to do with the forces involved
choices.explanation: Momentum conservation is directly explained BY the internal-force cancellation (Newton's Third Law) -- the forces are very much relevant to why conservation holds.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The objects don't actually exert forces on each other during a collision
choices.explanation: The objects absolutely do exert (often large) forces on each other during a collision -- that's exactly what changes each object's individual momentum.

explanation: The collision forces between the two objects are an internal Newton's Third Law pair, which cancel out for the system's total momentum.

stem: A system consists of two objects with a total momentum of 30 kg·m/s. If no external forces act on the system, what is the total momentum after any internal collisions or interactions between the two objects?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Still 30 kg·m/s
choices.explanation: With no external forces, the total momentum of the system remains constant, regardless of what internal interactions (like collisions) occur between the two objects.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 0 kg·m/s, since internal collisions always cancel momentum
choices.explanation: Internal collisions don't cancel the SYSTEM's total momentum to zero -- conservation means it stays at its original value, 30 kg·m/s.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It depends on whether the collision is elastic or inelastic
choices.explanation: Momentum conservation applies to BOTH elastic and inelastic collisions equally -- only kinetic energy conservation depends on collision type.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It cannot be determined without more information
choices.explanation: It CAN be determined -- with no external forces, momentum conservation guarantees the total stays at 30 kg·m/s, regardless of the details of the internal interaction.

explanation: With no external forces, total system momentum remains constant at 30 kg·m/s regardless of internal interactions.

stem: What distinguishes an "elastic" collision from an "inelastic" collision?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In an elastic collision, kinetic energy is conserved; in an inelastic collision, some kinetic energy is converted to other forms (like heat or sound)
choices.explanation: This is the standard distinction: elastic collisions conserve KE, inelastic collisions don't (though momentum is conserved in both).

choices.label: B
choices.text: In an elastic collision, momentum is conserved; in an inelastic collision, it is not
choices.explanation: Momentum is conserved in BOTH types of collisions (given no external force) -- the distinguishing factor is kinetic energy conservation, not momentum.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Elastic collisions only happen between identical objects
choices.explanation: Elastic collisions can happen between objects of any mass -- the defining feature is kinetic energy conservation, not the objects being identical.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inelastic collisions never actually occur in nature
choices.explanation: Inelastic collisions are extremely common in the real world (e.g., car crashes, a ball of clay hitting a wall) -- perfectly elastic collisions are actually the idealized, rarer case.

explanation: Elastic collisions conserve kinetic energy; inelastic collisions convert some KE into other forms of energy.

stem: What happens to the two objects in a "perfectly inelastic" collision?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They stick together and move with a common final velocity
choices.explanation: A perfectly inelastic collision is defined by the two objects sticking together after impact, moving as one combined mass.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They bounce off each other and both conserve kinetic energy
choices.explanation: This describes an ELASTIC collision, not a perfectly inelastic one.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They pass through each other unaffected
choices.explanation: Objects don't pass through each other unaffected in any real physical collision -- and this doesn't describe a perfectly inelastic collision at all.

choices.label: D
choices.text: One object disappears entirely
choices.explanation: Both objects continue to exist after the collision -- they simply move together as a combined mass, rather than one vanishing.

explanation: In a perfectly inelastic collision, the two objects stick together and move with a shared final velocity.

stem: A 4 kg cart moving at 6 m/s collides with a 2 kg cart moving at -3 m/s (opposite direction). They stick together. What is their combined velocity after the collision?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 3 m/s
choices.explanation: By conservation of momentum: (4)(6)+(2)(-3) = (4+2)v_f, so 24-6=18=6v_f, giving v_f=3 m/s.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This is half the correct value, likely from a division error.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This doesn't correctly compute the net initial momentum (18 kg·m/s) before dividing by the combined mass.

choices.label: D
choices.text: 6 m/s
choices.explanation: This ignores the second cart's opposing momentum entirely.

explanation: Total momentum before = (4)(6)+(2)(-3) = 24-6 = 18 kg·m/s. After sticking: v_f = 18/6 = 3 m/s.

stem: Using the same scenario as before ($m_1=4$ kg at 6 m/s, $m_2=2$ kg at -3 m/s, sticking together at 3 m/s), compare the total kinetic energy before and after the collision.

choices.label: A
choices.text: KE before = 81 J, KE after = 27 J -- kinetic energy decreased, confirming this was an inelastic collision
choices.explanation: KE_before = (1/2)(4)(6²)+(1/2)(2)(3²) = 72+9 = 81 J. KE_after = (1/2)(6)(3²) = 27 J. Since KE decreased, this confirms the collision was inelastic.

choices.label: B
choices.text: KE before = 81 J, KE after = 81 J -- kinetic energy was conserved
choices.explanation: Kinetic energy is NOT conserved here (a perfectly inelastic collision) -- it decreases from 81 J to 27 J.

choices.label: C
choices.text: KE before = 27 J, KE after = 81 J -- kinetic energy increased
choices.explanation: This has the values backward, and kinetic energy cannot spontaneously increase in a collision without an external energy source.

choices.label: D
choices.text: KE cannot be computed without additional information
choices.explanation: KE can be directly computed from each object's mass and velocity (KE=(1/2)mv²) -- no additional information is needed here.

explanation: KE_before = 72+9 = 81 J; KE_after = (1/2)(6)(9) = 27 J -- confirming kinetic energy is lost in this inelastic collision.

stem: In a perfectly elastic, head-on collision between a moving object and an identical stationary object (equal masses), what happens to their velocities?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The moving object comes to rest, and the previously stationary object moves off with the first object's original velocity (they "exchange" velocities)
choices.explanation: This is a well-known special case: for equal masses in an elastic collision, the velocities are completely exchanged.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Both objects move off together at half the original velocity
choices.explanation: This describes a perfectly INELASTIC collision (sticking together), not an elastic one.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both objects continue at the original velocity, unaffected by the collision
choices.explanation: A collision necessarily changes at least one object's velocity -- they don't simply continue unaffected.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The moving object bounces straight back at the same speed, and the stationary object stays at rest
choices.explanation: This isn't consistent with momentum conservation for EQUAL masses -- the correct elastic-collision result is a full velocity exchange.

explanation: For an elastic collision between equal masses (one moving, one at rest), the velocities are exactly exchanged.

stem: Is momentum conserved in an elastic collision?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Yes -- momentum is conserved in ALL collisions, elastic or inelastic, as long as there's no external force
choices.explanation: Momentum conservation applies universally to isolated collisions, regardless of whether kinetic energy is also conserved (elastic) or not (inelastic).

choices.label: B
choices.text: No -- only kinetic energy is conserved in elastic collisions, not momentum
choices.explanation: BOTH momentum and kinetic energy are conserved in elastic collisions -- momentum conservation isn't limited to inelastic collisions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Momentum is only conserved in inelastic collisions
choices.explanation: Momentum is conserved in elastic collisions too -- it's a universal principle for isolated systems, regardless of collision type.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Momentum conservation doesn't apply to collisions at all
choices.explanation: Momentum conservation is one of the most fundamental principles used to analyze ALL types of collisions.

explanation: Momentum is conserved in all collisions (elastic or inelastic) as long as there's no external force.

stem: A ball of clay is thrown at a wall and sticks to it. What type of collision is this, and what happens to the clay's kinetic energy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A perfectly inelastic collision -- the clay's kinetic energy is converted mostly into heat and deformation energy as it flattens against the wall
choices.explanation: Sticking upon impact is the hallmark of a perfectly inelastic collision; the KE is converted to other forms (heat, sound, deformation), not conserved.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A perfectly elastic collision -- all kinetic energy is conserved
choices.explanation: This is the opposite of what happens -- clay sticking to a wall is a classic example of a perfectly INELASTIC collision, where KE is NOT conserved.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No collision occurs since the wall doesn't move
choices.explanation: A collision absolutely occurs -- the wall not moving (much) doesn't mean there's no collision, just that the wall's effective mass is very large.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The clay's kinetic energy is unaffected by sticking to the wall
choices.explanation: The clay's kinetic energy essentially goes to zero (since it stops), converted into other forms of energy like heat and deformation.

explanation: This is a perfectly inelastic collision; the clay's kinetic energy converts mostly to heat and deformation energy.

stem: In real-world collisions (like most car crashes), are they typically closer to perfectly elastic or perfectly inelastic?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Closer to inelastic -- some kinetic energy is generally lost to heat, sound, and deformation in most real collisions
choices.explanation: Most real-world macroscopic collisions are at least partially inelastic; perfectly elastic collisions are an idealization more closely approximated by things like billiard balls or gas molecules.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Closer to elastic -- kinetic energy is almost perfectly conserved in most real collisions
choices.explanation: Most macroscopic real-world collisions (like car crashes) lose significant kinetic energy to deformation, heat, and sound -- they are NOT close to perfectly elastic.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It's impossible for a real collision to be either elastic or inelastic
choices.explanation: Real collisions can be reasonably well-approximated as elastic or inelastic; both categories are genuinely useful and applicable models.

choices.label: D
choices.text: All real collisions are perfectly elastic by definition
choices.explanation: This isn't correct -- most real-world collisions involve some energy loss (to heat, sound, deformation), making them at least partially inelastic.

explanation: Most real-world collisions (like car crashes) are closer to inelastic, losing kinetic energy to heat, sound, and deformation.

stem: What is the "center of mass" of a system of objects?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The mass-weighted average position of all the objects in the system
choices.explanation: The center of mass is the point representing the average position of mass in a system, weighted by each object's mass.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The location of the heaviest single object in the system
choices.explanation: The center of mass is a weighted AVERAGE across all objects, not simply the position of the single heaviest one.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The geometric center of the system, regardless of mass distribution
choices.explanation: The center of mass depends on how mass is distributed, not just pure geometry -- it can differ from the simple geometric center if masses aren't uniform.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A fixed point that never changes, regardless of how the objects move
choices.explanation: The center of mass CAN move as the objects in the system move or if an external force acts -- it isn't necessarily fixed.

explanation: The center of mass is the mass-weighted average position of a system's objects.

stem: Two masses lie on the x-axis: $m_1=2$ kg at $x=0$ m, and $m_2=4$ kg at $x=6$ m. Where is their center of mass?

choices.label: A
choices.text: x = 4 m

choices.label: B
choices.text: x = 3 m
choices.explanation: This is the simple (unweighted) midpoint, not the mass-weighted center of mass.

choices.label: C
choices.text: x = 6 m
choices.explanation: This is just the position of the heavier mass, not the weighted average of both positions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: x = 2 m
choices.explanation: This doesn't correctly weight each position by its corresponding mass.

explanation: x_cm = (2(0)+4(6))/6 = 24/6 = 4 m -- closer to the heavier mass, as expected.

stem: Why does a system's center of mass end up closer to the more massive object (when there are two objects of different mass)?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Because the center of mass formula weights each object's position by its mass, so a larger mass "pulls" the average position toward itself
choices.explanation: The weighted-average nature of the center of mass formula means more massive objects have proportionally more influence on the resulting position.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It doesn't -- the center of mass is always exactly at the geometric midpoint regardless of mass
choices.explanation: The center of mass generally is NOT at the simple geometric midpoint unless the masses happen to be equal -- it shifts toward the more massive object.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Because gravity pulls the center of mass toward the heavier object
choices.explanation: This isn't about gravitational attraction between the objects -- it's purely a mathematical consequence of the mass-weighted averaging formula.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Because the less massive object doesn't count in the calculation at all
choices.explanation: The less massive object DOES count -- it's just weighted less heavily than the more massive object, not excluded entirely.

explanation: The center of mass formula weights each position by mass, so a larger mass shifts the average position toward itself.

stem: What determines how the center of mass of a system moves over time?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Only the NET EXTERNAL force on the system -- internal forces (like those in a collision) don't affect the center of mass's motion
choices.explanation: Internal forces cancel by Newton's Third Law, so they can't accelerate the system's center of mass; only external forces can.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Both internal and external forces equally affect the center of mass's motion
choices.explanation: Internal forces cancel out (Newton's Third Law pairs) and have NO net effect on the center of mass's motion -- only external forces matter.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Only internal forces determine the center of mass's motion
choices.explanation: This is backward -- internal forces cancel out and don't affect the center of mass; only EXTERNAL forces do.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The center of mass never moves, regardless of any forces
choices.explanation: The center of mass absolutely can move, if there's a net EXTERNAL force acting on the system (e.g., gravity on a projectile).

explanation: Only net external forces affect the center of mass's motion; internal forces cancel out (Newton's Third Law) and have no effect on it.

stem: A spinning wrench is thrown through the air, tumbling as it flies. What path does its center of mass follow?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A smooth parabolic path, exactly as if it were a simple projectile (point mass) under gravity -- even though the rest of the wrench tumbles chaotically
choices.explanation: Regardless of how an extended object tumbles or rotates, its center of mass follows the same simple projectile-motion path a point mass would, under the net external force (gravity).

choices.label: B
choices.text: A chaotic, tumbling path, mirroring the wrench's rotation
choices.explanation: While the rest of the wrench tumbles chaotically, the CENTER OF MASS specifically follows a smooth parabolic path -- rotation doesn't affect the center of mass's own trajectory.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A straight horizontal line
choices.explanation: Under gravity, the center of mass follows a curved (parabolic) path, not a straight horizontal line, just like ordinary projectile motion.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It cannot be determined for a tumbling object
choices.explanation: It CAN be determined -- the center of mass always follows simple projectile motion under the net external force, regardless of the object's internal rotation or tumbling.

explanation: Even for a tumbling extended object, its center of mass follows the same smooth parabolic path a simple point-mass projectile would.

stem: Three equal masses $m$ are placed at $x=0$ m, $x=3$ m, and $x=6$ m. Where is the system's center of mass?

choices.label: A
choices.text: x = 3 m

stem: Two ice skaters, initially at rest and holding hands, push off from each other. What happens to the center of mass of the two-skater system (ignoring friction) after they push apart?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It stays in the same place, since there's no external horizontal force on the system
choices.explanation: The push-off force between the skaters is internal; with no external horizontal force (ignoring friction), the center of mass of the system doesn't move.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It moves toward whichever skater is more massive
choices.explanation: The center of mass doesn't shift toward either skater after they push apart -- it stays fixed, since the push-off is purely an internal force.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It moves in the direction both skaters end up moving
choices.explanation: The skaters move in OPPOSITE directions from each other (by momentum conservation) -- there's no single common direction for the center of mass to move toward.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It accelerates continuously outward
choices.explanation: With no external force, the center of mass cannot accelerate -- it remains exactly where it was.

explanation: Since the push-off is an internal force with no external horizontal force on the system, the center of mass remains stationary.
